summary: Reports on an IAB workshop at the University of Cambridge in December 2013 on Internet technology adoption and transition. It examines economic models, especially at the waist of the hourglass in the protocol stack, with no single set of recommendations.

plainLanguage.summary: Experts met to discuss why some new internet ideas catch on and others do not. This is the report.

questions: what factors make internet protocols successful
why has ipv6 adoption been slow
how does bundling affect protocol adoption
what role do incentives play in protocol deployment
subtitle: Workshop report examining how internet protocols succeed or fail to be adopted.

tldr.problem: New internet protocols often fail to be widely adopted despite technical merit, and success depends on complex interactions between design, deployment strategies, incentives, and economic factors—not just engineering.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB workshop brought together researchers, operators, and economists to examine case studies in protocol adoption (IPv6, DNSSEC, Bitcoin, HTTP/2) and discuss economic models, bundling strategies, and incentive structures that affect deployment.
tldr.outcome: The workshop identified patterns including the importance of direct benefit to participants, network effects, incentive alignment, and the need to bridge academic research and IETF standardization. No single formula emerged but several research directions were highlighted for further exploration.

today: RFC 7305 is an Informational report. Its observations on protocol success remain relevant: IPv6 adoption continues slowly despite over two decades of effort; DNSSEC deployment remains limited; and the IRTF has not pursued major research groups on protocol economics. However, the workshop's emphasis on incentive alignment and deployment strategy has influenced thinking in the IETF, particularly in discussions of DNS privacy, HTTPS adoption, and emerging protocol standards.

sections.title: Why Protocols Succeed and Fail
sections.content:
The internet's protocol stack has an hourglass shape: at the narrow middle sits IP, with many protocols above it (TCP, HTTP, DNS) and below it (Ethernet, fiber optics). This design has proven remarkably successful. Yet many promising protocols struggle to deploy widely. IPv6, despite being designed as the successor to IPv4, took decades to see meaningful adoption. DNSSEC adds security to DNS but has been deployed very slowly. Meanwhile, protocols designed without IETF standardization, like HTTP, have evolved steadily.

The workshop considered a central question: can engineering alone explain adoption patterns? The answer is largely no. Successful protocols require not only good design but also deployment incentives, economic alignment, and strategies that allow early adopters to benefit. In the presence of network effects (where a protocol becomes more valuable as more people use it), deployment barriers become especially difficult to overcome. Technologies like Bitcoin, which offer direct monetary reward to early participants, succeed despite significant obstacles. Email succeeded partly by offering simple bridges to non-Internet email systems. These insights point beyond pure technology to strategy and economics.
sections.plainLanguage: New network ideas need more than clever engineering to win. They need to give early users a reason to switch, work with existing systems, and overcome the advantage of whatever's already popular.

sections.title: Economic Models of Adoption
sections.content:
The workshop examined several economic frameworks for understanding adoption. Bundling can help when one technology provides immediate value while bundling it with a technology that needs critical mass to become valuable. An example is DANE, which depends on DNSSEC adoption; bundling them together can help both. However, bundling can also harm adoption if users perceive the bundled technologies as competing for resources.

Direct benefit to participants proved critical. Bitcoin succeeded despite legal and technical uncertainties because miners and early adopters earn coins. The workshop noted that if a protocol imposes costs on other systems (such as requiring router upgrades), mechanisms must exist to incentivize those third parties. Sweden's .SE registry provided financial incentives for DNSSEC deployment at registrars and registrants, removing both financial and technical barriers. The Internet's success partly came from protocols offering clear benefits to end users and network operators simultaneously.

The workshop also discussed the importance of interface compatibility. Protocols that bridge old and new systems (email connecting Internet and non-Internet systems) succeed more readily than those requiring wholesale replacement. The concept of happy eyeballs—trying multiple mechanisms and using the best one—was highlighted as a practical deployment pattern that avoids forcing a single technology choice.
sections.plainLanguage: People adopt new network ideas when they personally benefit right away, when it works with systems they already use, and when someone rewards them for being early. Money and convenience matter as much as cleverness.

sections.title: Standards, Complexity, and Research
sections.content:
A major theme was the gap between academic research and IETF standardization. Researchers developing IPv6 transition technologies or mobile traffic offloading solutions encountered resistance in both 3GPP and IETF standardization bodies. In one case, researchers jumped to proposing solutions without fully explaining the problem, missing buy-in from standardizers. The workshop discussed whether IETF working groups could benefit from graduate student involvement in document review, building research understanding of real-world standardization processes.

The complexity of designed systems emerged as a concern. The internet's distributed, layered design is robust yet fragile—highly efficient systems can break unexpectedly and prove hard to evolve. The workshop explored whether techniques from systems biology (where adenosine triphosphate plays a central role similar to IP's role in the internet) offer insights for engineers. One tentative conclusion was that network management itself deserves more research attention.

The workshop also examined the question of whether the current protocol stack serves all populations equally. Constraints like bandwidth availability, power consumption, and connectivity models in developing regions might require different architectural assumptions. Work on Lowest Common Denominator Networking (LCDNet) was discussed as exploring alternative hourglass designs for these environments.
sections.plainLanguage: Making new network technology work is not just about having good researchers and good standards organizations. They need to talk to each other, and we need to think about whether today's design assumptions fit everywhere.

sections.title: Challenges and Future Work
sections.content:
The workshop addressed routing security and the next generation of TLS as ongoing challenges. The tragedy of the commons applies to inter-domain routing: while all operators benefit from secure routing, each operator benefits if others implement protections. The Internet Society's work with operators involves building shared understanding of risks and benefits to break this deadlock. The workshop concluded that no single technical solution exists; instead, identifying key players and aligning their incentives is the real challenge.

For TLS, the workshop noted that old implementations still use outdated versions and encryption methods (such as Triple DES), slowing migration to newer, stronger versions. Testing platforms and incentive mechanisms for deployment might help, but the workshop acknowledged that making the perfect successor (rather than iteratively improving the incumbent) can hinder progress.

Workshop participants suggested several outcomes: the IAB should apply RFC 5218 (on protocol success factors) when reviewing Birds of a Feather sessions and working group charters. Track and publicize protocol success stories. Consider standardizing the DNSSEC DS-key provisioning interface between parent and child zones. The IRTF might pursue research groups on protocol alternatives for constrained environments and economic models of protocol adoption. Finally, partners like ICANN and Regional Internet Registries can continue using their policy mechanisms to encourage deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: Getting routing security right requires everyone to care about the problem together. Standards organizations and researchers should work more closely. Tracking what works and what fails helps the next generation of protocols.
